posts.t: Hi be70isme, I think you've got the general idea if you are just trying to read price inside the box. If I was trading it, I wouldn't be messing around inside the box, I would be looking to the edges of the box/flag. The biggest challenge in reading price, is determining the engulf from the fakeout. If price engulfs below a demand (DBR) and into a flag limit, then it may be an FO. Price must be read in context using all the timeframes.

I started doing some FL HW on forextester with usd/cad and saw this PA that I didn't understand.

Also I have been kind of foggy on the origin concept. I feel it is important to understand where the origin is since sometimes the whole point of the PA we are seeing is to make it back there to fill the rest of their orders. So knowing where and when it gets hit can be a very important piece to the puzzle.

Other than that the questions are on the charts. I included a clean chart so in case you want to draw you don't have to draw around my stuff. Ty for any insight.
You've gotten the sequence a bit off there:)

Thanks for setting me straight IF.

I have been looking at price in blocks. With the larger blocks taking precedent over the smaller blocks. I see the larger blocks as HTF and the smaller blocks as LTF. This chart shows what I mean.

I guess that is all fine and good if we are trying to make art from the chart. But the object here is to find where the selling pressure is, and in this case the sell orders were contained in the "LTF" box. Even though the FTR itself (the real one on IF's chart) was only a failure to return to the immediate supply above, the supply contained within was strong enough to engulf the FL holding up the "HTF" box. And even though the FTR in control was located within the "LTF" box, it "represents" the intent not to return to the PA contained in the "HTF" box. Which means we start our sequence there. I hope all that makes sense.

Here is another chart showing why I didn't consider the real FTR important.

I think I get it, but a quick explanation or up to confirm would be great.:)

Hi guys,

Would you be comfortable taking this trade again on return? The first time back missed entry by 1/10th of a pip and "technically" didn't touch the zone. I have a 5 digit broker, so I'm not sure if it would have actually touched on a 4 digit broker. Would you consider the zone stronger or weaker upon the next return. I can see it both ways.

Stronger because there was so much selling pressure that price barely flicked the zone. That could suggest that the next time it might go a little bit deeper before it gets pushed down, but that there are still plenty of sell orders in that area.

Weaker because the approach was due to a news event causing some serious buying right up into the zone allowing the IT's to fill a LOT of sell orders. How many are left? We'll never know exactly until price eventually returns.

What are your views?

Hello, not sure if this the right place to ask. I think I so far have a fairly decent understanding of what S/D zones are and how to spot them. However, sometimes zones I would regard as "good" zones are simply ignored. Attached an image of a recent supply zone in EURUSD ignored (marked green) which just puzzles me, because I can not even see a small reaction to it on the 1 minute chart when price rallied through it like a hot knife through butter. The only explanation I can come up with is that the zone was on a level where price was ranging around for some time already, and that made it less important? (marked in pink) The picture is the 30min, but it does not make more sense to me on higher TF either.

So I thought I would continue with the next topics in the homework section to see if I can get a better understanding why some zones are ignored and others are not, but I really struggle to understand what a compression is and how to spot it. From what I understand, CP is price going back to very recent S/D zones to clear pending orders, so that price can move freely through this area because there are no or only little orders left. What I fail to grasp is how this is different to pirce simply reacting to S/D zones, just on smaller timeframe, or maybe better: in a shorter time. Because price clearing an area to break through only makes sense to me in hindsight. To define a CP, is it important how the candles "look"? So for example is CP defined by smaller candles where the range of these candles is not much different from those preceding them?
